This reproductive schedule is observed under favorable thermal conditions averaging 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which corresponds to the species' active metabolic period in its tropical understory habitat. The eggs, deposited in a cup nest concealed within dense vegetation, are incubated by the female alone over a developmentally critical period. Hatching occurs after an incubation period of roughly 14 days [ab = roughly 14 days], though this stage is tightly linked to the microclimate of the nest, which is maintained at a markedly cooler incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This temperature differential between the incubation environment and the ambient conditions experienced by post-hatching individuals reflects the thermal buffering provided by the nest structure and the female's attentive brooding.

At the moment of hatching, the altricial neonate has a wet weight at birth of approximately 2.65 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.65 grams], a modest mass that represents only a small fraction of the ultimate adult size. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, in contrast, is around 3.95 grams [Ww0 = around 3.95 grams], indicating that the egg itself is heavier than the hatchling it contains, a discrepancy accounted for by the loss of albumen water and the metabolic costs of embryonic development. This pattern of a relatively large egg yielding a smaller hatchling is typical of many songbirds and reflects the allocation of resources to yolk reserves before laying. The nestling period is characterized by rapid tissue accretion, fueled by the constant provisioning of insects by both parents, a strategy that supports the swift increase in body mass that will eventually lead to fledging.

The subsequent developmental milestones of the nestling are also governed by the prevailing thermal conditions of the breeding season. Under the typical active-phase temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which defines the metabolic environment of the growing chick, the time since birth at fledging is a brief 12.5 days [tx = 12.5 days]. This rapid development from a helpless neonate to a flight-capable juvenile is an adaptation to the high predation pressure typical of tropical forests, where a prolonged nestling period would incur unacceptable risk of loss. The fledgling, though capable of short flights, remains dependent on its parents for food for several additional weeks as it refines its foraging skills. Following this period of nutritional dependence, the immature bird enters a juvenile stage that is characterized by a drabber plumage compared to the striking black and white of the adult male.

The trajectory toward sexual maturity unfolds over a period of several weeks after the young bird becomes independent. Puberty in the White-rumped shama is attained at a time since birth of 37.5 days [tp = 37.5 days] when the individual is maintained at the ambient metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. At this point, the juvenile undergoes a complete pre-basic molt, acquiring the definitive adult plumage, and the gonads become fully functional. Total body mass at this stage is still increasing, as the bird has not yet reached its asymptotic adult size. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of 26.7 grams [Wwi = 26.7 grams], a value considerably lower than that of males, which reach a maximum adult body mass of approximately 31.75 grams [Wwi = approximately 31.75 grams]. This sexual size dimorphism, though modest in absolute terms, is consistent across populations and is likely linked to the sexual selection pressures generated by male song.

The first successful brood is initiated relatively soon after the achievement of gonadal maturity. At an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] in their preferred lowland forest habitat, the time since birth at first brood is recorded at 365 days [tR = 365 days]. This delay of nearly a full year between reaching physiological puberty and producing the first clutch likely reflects the time required for a young bird to establish a territory, attract a mate, and accumulate sufficient body condition to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The species' lifespan is notably extended for a passerine of its body size, with the maximum recorded longevity reaching 7 years [am = 7 years] under continuous exposure to the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively long life, combined with a moderate annual reproductive rate, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high fecundity.
